title: Heritage walk in Udaipur: City Palace, ghats and old city
seo_title: Heritage Walk in Udaipur: Historical Places, Lakes, Museums
meta_description: Plan a heritage walk in Udaipur: City Palace, Jagdish Temple, Gangaur Ghat, Bagore ki Haveli, the lakes, museums, and Kumbhalgarh and Chittorgarh nearby.
summary: A heritage walk in Udaipur follows the old city on the east shore of Lake Pichola: the City Palace complex, Jagdish Temple (1651), the havelis and ghats around Gangaur Ghat, and Bagore ki Haveli. Udaipur is also the base for Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh, two of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan on the UNESCO list.

paras: Udaipur was the last capital of the Sisodia rulers of Mewar, one of the oldest ruling houses in Rajasthan. The city was planned around water: Lake Pichola, Fateh Sagar and a chain of smaller lakes and dams that stored monsoon rain in a dry region. Palaces, ghats, temples and havelis face the water, and the old city still keeps its gates and much of its street plan.

For students the city makes clear how a court capital worked. The palace, the royal temple, the merchant havelis, the craft lanes and the ghats where people bathed and washed all sit within a short walk. It also introduces Mewar's longer history, which is spread across forts such as Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh within a few hours' drive.

sections.h2: Layers of history in and around Udaipur
paras: Long before the city, the region had early farming settlements. Ahar, on the eastern edge of Udaipur, gives its name to the Ahar-Banas culture, a Chalcolithic farming culture dated to roughly the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, known for its black-and-red pottery and copper working. The small site museum at Ahar shows finds from the excavations.

Mewar's earlier capitals were Nagda and then Chittorgarh. After Akbar's siege of Chittor in 1567 to 1568, Maharana Udai Singh II moved the court to the new city he had begun near Lake Pichola, traditionally dated to 1559. His son Maharana Pratap fought the Mughals at Haldighati in 1576. Mewar later came to terms with the Mughals in 1615, and in 1818 signed a treaty with the British.

The City Palace grew over about three centuries as successive Maharanas added courtyards and wings, which is why its parts differ so much. Smaller monuments include the Jagdish Temple of 1651, a Nagara temple in the Maru-Gurjara style, and Bagore ki Haveli, an 18th century minister's mansion. Our explainer on [Nagara temple architecture](nagara-temple-architecture.html) helps read the temple.

sections.h2: What you see on an Udaipur heritage walk
paras: The walk begins at the City Palace's Badi Pol and Tripolia gates and looks at how the palace is planned as a fortress facing the town and a pleasure palace facing the lake. Inside, the museum galleries show mirror work, paintings in the Mewar style and armour. From the palace the route climbs to the Jagdish Temple, then drops through lanes of painters, silversmiths and small shrines to Gangaur Ghat and Bagore ki Haveli.

Look for evidence of how the city managed water: the stepped ghats, the overflow channels, and inscriptions recording who built a dam or tank. A short boat crossing gives a view of Jag Mandir and Jag Niwas (the Lake Palace), both built as royal retreats in the 17th and 18th centuries. Our guide to [forts of India](forts-of-india.html) and the wider guide to [heritage sites in Rajasthan](heritage-sites-in-rajasthan.html) put Udaipur's palace in context.

sections.h2: Day trips: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranakpur and Eklingji
paras: Chittorgarh (about 2 hours by road) and Kumbhalgarh (about 2 to 2.5 hours) are both part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, a UNESCO site since 2013. Chittor has the Vijaya Stambha (Tower of Victory) built under Rana Kumbha in the 15th century, palaces and Jain temples; Kumbhalgarh has one of the longest fortification walls in India. The Jain temple at Ranakpur, built in the 15th century with more than a thousand carved pillars, is near Kumbhalgarh. Eklingji and the older temples of Nagda are about 25 kilometres north of the city.

We arrange Udaipur walks for your group, planned with you. For a longer trip, [Forts of Rajasthan](forts-of-rajasthan.html) is a study tour that links Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and other hill forts with an archaeologist, and the lecture [Understanding Indian temple architecture](understanding-indian-temple-architecture.html) prepares a group well for Ranakpur and Nagda.

sections.h2: Udaipur heritage walk for schools and groups
paras: The old city route is about 2 kilometres but has steep sections near the Jagdish Temple and the palace. It suits classes 5 and above. Start early in the morning, before the palace gets crowded, and allow 90 minutes inside the City Palace Museum. The ghats are best in the evening light. Forts need a full day with a vehicle and include long walks on uneven ground.

stops.name: City Palace, Udaipur
stops.period: From the 16th century, enlarged to the 19th
stops.note: Courtyards, mirror rooms and galleries built by successive Maharanas; now partly a museum.

stops.name: Tripolia Gate
stops.note: Triple-arched gate into the palace, where rulers were traditionally weighed against gold and silver for charity.

stops.name: Jagdish Temple
stops.note: Large Nagara temple built by Maharana Jagat Singh I, with a carved plinth of elephants and riders.

stops.name: Bagore ki Haveli
stops.note: A minister's mansion on Gangaur Ghat with over a hundred rooms, now a museum.

stops.name: Gangaur Ghat
stops.note: Stepped ghat on Lake Pichola with a triple-arched gateway, used for the Gangaur festival.

stops.name: Lake Pichola
stops.period: Tank from the 14th century, enlarged by Udai Singh II
stops.note: The lake the city was built around; a boat gives views of the palace from the water.

stops.name: Jag Mandir
stops.note: Island palace where Prince Khurram (later Shah Jahan) is said to have taken refuge in the 1620s.

stops.name: Lake Palace (Jag Niwas)
stops.note: Royal summer palace on an island, now a hotel; seen from the shore or the boat.

stops.name: Fateh Sagar Lake
stops.note: Lake rebuilt by Maharana Fateh Singh after a flood, connected to Pichola by a canal.

stops.name: Saheliyon ki Bari
stops.note: Garden with fountains and pools for the royal women; vehicle or long walk from the old city.

stops.name: Ahar Cenotaphs and site museum
stops.note: Royal cenotaphs of Mewar beside the excavated Ahar mound and its small museum.

stops.name: Eklingji and Nagda temples
stops.period: Nagda temples about 10th century; Eklingji rebuilt later
stops.note: Mewar's family temple and the older Sas-Bahu temples at Nagda; vehicle needed.

stops.name: Chittorgarh Fort
stops.note: UNESCO hill fort with the Vijaya Stambha and Rani Padmini's palace; vehicle needed.

stops.name: Kumbhalgarh Fort
stops.note: Built under Rana Kumbha, with a very long wall and many temples; vehicle needed.

routes.name: Palace to the ghats on foot
The lakes
routes.length: About 2.5 hours with a boat and a short drive

museums.name: City Palace Museum
museums.note: Galleries of Mewar painting, arms, royal objects and restored rooms such as the Mor Chowk.

museums.name: Ahar Archaeological Museum
museums.note: Small government museum with finds from the Ahar excavations and early sculpture from Mewar.

museums.name: Bagore ki Haveli Museum
museums.note: Restored rooms, costume and turban collections, and an evening folk performance.

museums.name: Bharatiya Lok Kala Mandal
museums.note: Folk art museum with puppets, masks and instruments from Rajasthan.

best_time: October to March. Summers are very hot; after a good monsoon (August to September) the lakes are full and the city is at its best, though forts can be slippery.

faq.q: What are the main historical places in Udaipur?
faq.a: The City Palace, Jagdish Temple, Bagore ki Haveli, Gangaur Ghat, Jag Mandir, the Lake Palace, Fateh Sagar, Saheliyon ki Bari and the Ahar cenotaphs. Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh forts and the Ranakpur temple are within a few hours.
Maharana Udai Singh II of Mewar, traditionally around 1559. The city became the main Mewar capital after Akbar captured Chittorgarh in 1568.

faq.q: Is Udaipur a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.a: The city is not on the list, but two Mewar forts that are easy day trips, Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh, are part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, inscribed in 2013.

faq.q: Is the Udaipur heritage walk suitable for schools?
faq.a: Yes, for classes 5 and above. The old city has some steep lanes and steps. Younger children manage a shorter version focused on the palace and the ghats.

faq.q: Which museum in Udaipur is best for students?
faq.a: The City Palace Museum for court life and painting, and the Ahar museum for the region's early farming communities. Together they show two very different periods.

posts.hook: Udaipur sits on a 4,000 year old farming village.
posts.caption: Ahar, on the city's edge, gives its name to a Chalcolithic culture of copper workers and farmers. The royal cenotaphs stand right beside the excavated mound.
From a boat on Lake Pichola the City Palace looks like a fortress on one side and a pleasure palace on the other. Then walk the ghats to see how ordinary people used the same lake.
